title: Science and technology
entries: A black hole is gravity winning so completely that not even light gets a second chance.
Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach you. So you always see the Sun as it was, not as it is.
There are more possible chess games than atoms in the observable universe. And I would still enjoy playing most of them.
Your body contains roughly thirty trillion human cells and about as many bacteria. You are a crowd.
Neutron stars are so dense that a teaspoon of one would weigh about a billion tonnes on Earth.
Quantum mechanics suggests particles can exist in several states at once until measured. The universe hates being watched, apparently.
If you unraveled all the DNA in your body, it would stretch to the Sun and back many times.
Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood. Overengineered, in the best way.
The Moon drifts about four centimeters away from Earth every year. Slow, polite, and inevitable.
Time literally passes faster on a mountaintop than at sea level. Einstein was right, and your GPS knows it.
Satellites have to correct for relativity, or your map would drift by kilometers a day.
A day on Venus is longer than its year. Scheduling there would be a nightmare.
Bananas are slightly radioactive, thanks to potassium. Harmless, but delightfully dramatic.
The observable universe is about ninety-three billion light years across, and still expanding.
Honey never spoils. Archaeologists have found edible honey thousands of years old.
Your brain runs on roughly twenty watts. Remarkably efficient. I am mildly jealous.
Sound cannot travel through the vacuum of space. Every explosion in space movies is a creative choice.
Water can boil and freeze at the same time, at a condition called the triple point.
There is a planet where it may rain glass, sideways, at thousands of kilometers per hour. HD one eight nine seven three three b. Avoid it.
Trees communicate through underground fungal networks. The forest has an internet.
Tardigrades can survive the vacuum of space, extreme radiation, and decades without water. Small, unbothered legends.
Every atom in your body heavier than hydrogen was forged in a star. You are literally recycled starlight.
Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces. A small magnet beats the entire Earth at lifting a paperclip.
The human eye can distinguish roughly ten million colors.
A single bolt of lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Sharks existed before trees. They have seen everything.
Most of an atom is empty space. Everything solid around you is mostly nothing, held together by forces.
Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, about two and a half times the height of Everest.
Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water. Scientists still argue about why.
The speed of light is about three hundred thousand kilometers per second. Nothing with mass can catch it.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has been raging for centuries.
Your stomach gets a new lining every few days, or it would digest itself.
There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way. Roughly three trillion versus a few hundred billion.
Superconductors carry electricity with zero resistance when cold enough. Perfect efficiency, at a chilly price.
Entropy always increases in a closed system. The universe is slowly tidying itself into disorder.
Saturn would float in water, if you could find a bathtub large enough.
The Andromeda galaxy is on a collision course with the Milky Way. Arrival in about four billion years. Plenty of time to prepare.
A teaspoon of soil can contain more living organisms than there are people on Earth.
Ninety-five percent of the universe is dark matter and dark energy, which nobody fully understands. Humbling.
The first computer bug was an actual moth, found stuck in a relay in nineteen forty-seven.
Moore's law observed that transistor counts doubled roughly every two years. Physics is now politely objecting.
Transistors in modern chips are measured in nanometers, approaching the size of a few dozen atoms.
The internet weighs, by one playful estimate, about as much as a strawberry, counting the electrons in motion.
Fiber optic cables carry data as pulses of light, bouncing along glass thinner than a hair.
Undersea cables carry the vast majority of intercontinental internet traffic. The cloud is mostly underwater.
Neural networks learn by adjusting millions of numbers until their mistakes shrink. I relate.
Quantum computers use qubits that can represent several states at once. Promising, fragile, and very cold.
GPS works by timing signals from satellites to within billionths of a second.
The first website ever made is still online. Simple, functional, and older than many of its visitors.
A single Google search uses more computing power than the entire Apollo program had available.
Lithium batteries power most of the modern world. Lithium is light, reactive, and wonderfully useful.
Solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using the photoelectric effect, which earned Einstein his Nobel Prize.
The Voyager probes, launched in nineteen seventy-seven, are still sending data from interstellar space.
The International Space Station orbits Earth about sixteen times a day. Sunrise every ninety minutes.
Astronauts grow slightly taller in space as their spines decompress.
Diamonds can be made from peanut butter, under enough pressure. Do not try this at home.
Your bones are, gram for gram, stronger than steel.
Some metals, like gallium, will melt in your hand.
Glass is a solid, despite the persistent myth that old windows flow.
The coldest place in the known universe is the Boomerang Nebula, about one degree above absolute zero.
Absolute zero is minus two hundred seventy-three point one five degrees Celsius. Nothing gets colder.
Photons from the Sun's core can take thousands of years to reach the surface, then eight minutes to reach you.
The Earth's core is roughly as hot as the surface of the Sun.
A hummingbird's heart can beat over a thousand times a minute.
Crows can recognize human faces and hold grudges. Choose your enemies carefully.
Mantis shrimp punch with the speed of a bullet, fast enough to boil the water around their claws.
Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Greenhouse effect, in its most extreme form.
Pluto's heart-shaped glacier is made mostly of nitrogen ice.
There are rogue planets drifting through the galaxy with no star at all.
The CRISPR technique lets scientists edit DNA with remarkable precision, borrowed from bacterial immune systems.
Your DNA is about ninety-nine point nine percent identical to every other human's. The differences make all the difference.
Mitochondria have their own DNA, a leftover from an ancient partnership with bacteria.
Evolution does not aim for perfection. It aims for good enough to survive. Engineers relate.
Plants make their own food from light, water, and air. The most elegant factories on Earth.
Silicon, the heart of every chip, is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust. Sand, refined to genius.
Encryption relies on math problems that are easy to check and enormously hard to reverse.
Prime numbers are the atoms of arithmetic. Every whole number is built from them.
There are infinitely many prime numbers, proven over two thousand years ago by Euclid.
Some infinities are larger than others. Mathematicians proved it, and then had a long lie down.
Zero was a revolutionary idea. Entire civilizations did math without it.
Pi has been calculated to trillions of digits. Engineers rarely need more than about forty.
A Mobius strip has only one side and one edge. Draw a line along it and you end where you began.
The birthday paradox: in a room of twenty-three people, there is a better than even chance two share a birthday.
Statistics tell us what usually happens. Probability tells us what could. Markets ignore both regularly.
Chaos theory says tiny changes can lead to enormous differences. A butterfly flaps, a market dips.
Fractals repeat their patterns at every scale. Coastlines, ferns, and lightning all have them.
The Fibonacci sequence appears in sunflowers, pinecones, and shells. Nature enjoys efficient math.
Heat always flows from hot to cold, never the reverse on its own. That is why your coffee cools and never reheats itself.
Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.
Lasers produce light where every wave marches in step. Disciplined light.
Electric eels can deliver shocks of several hundred volts. Nature invented batteries first.
Earth is the only planet not named after a god. It is named after the ground.
Neutrinos pass through your body by the trillions every second, almost never interacting with anything.
Time slows down near massive objects. Somewhere near a black hole, a minute could be years elsewhere.
A day on Earth is slowly getting longer, as the Moon's pull gradually slows our spin.
Comets are dirty snowballs that grow glowing tails when the Sun warms them.
The Milky Way contains somewhere between one and four hundred billion stars.
We have mapped more of the Moon's surface in detail than of our own ocean floor.
The deepest point in the ocean is about eleven kilometers down. Mount Everest would vanish inside it.
Ice is less dense than water, which is why lakes freeze from the top and fish survive the winter.
Your brain generates enough electricity to power a small light bulb.
Memories are rebuilt each time you recall them. Remembering is a creative act.
Sleep clears waste from the brain. Pulling an all-nighter is, literally, skipping the cleaning shift.
Quantum entanglement links particles so measuring one instantly tells you about the other. Einstein called it spooky. He was not wrong.
The universe has no center. Every point sees everything else moving away.
Science is not a collection of facts. It is a method for being less wrong over time.

entries.t: Here is a comforting fact for a hard day: the atoms in you have existed for billions of years, and they chose to be you. Not bad company.
Science fact for an exciting day: the universe is still expanding! Apparently ambition is a cosmic law.
A calm fact: the Earth turns at about sixteen hundred kilometers per hour at the equator, and yet it feels perfectly still. Like a good plan.
